In the language of India: *Saptaguṇaparivadanakathā*. In the language of Tibet: *Yon tan bdun yongs su brjod pa’i gtam* (The Discourse on Fully Expressing the Seven Qualities). Homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta!
One who desires various qualities should apply effort by resorting to the art of painting; without a seed, there is no possibility for a sprout to arise. [1]
One who desires various qualities based on many activities should perform them;
for without a seed, a sprout cannot arise.
When there is variety, one should undertake the collection of faultless qualities.
For a single fault has the power to corrupt many virtues; thus,
one should gather virtues while warding off faults, for a single fault destroys many virtues.
Long life, as well as health, physical beauty, good fortune, noble lineage,
wealth, and wisdom— these seven are the qualities proclaimed in the *Śubhasūtra*.
[3] Long life, likewise freedom from illness, physical form, good fortune, and lineage;
Wealth, wisdom, and the seven [jewels]—these qualities are taught in the sūtras.
Faults are the opposites of those; just as a single one among them can corrupt all the virtues, so too shall this be explained now. [4]
The opposite of that is a fault. Now, I shall explain how each of those [practices] gives rise to all virtuous qualities:
health, beauty, good fortune, noble lineage, wealth, and the perfection of knowledge.
Without a long life,
even an abundance of beauty, good fortune, noble birth, wealth,
and wisdom is like the ornaments of one condemned to execution.
Even these qualities, such as longevity, beauty, and so forth, decay for one who lacks freedom from illness,
like excellent women for an impotent man whose desires remain unfulfilled.
[6] Even these qualities, such as longevity, beauty, and so forth, decay for one who lacks freedom from illness.
[7] To see one who is formless, even if possessed of excellent qualities, is a source of revulsion; it is like seeing a supreme eunuch who possesses no virility,
or like the wives of kings looking upon the sage Vyāsa despite his abundance of virtues.
Even upon seeing one endowed with virtues, weariness arises in one who is ill-favored;
yet the full expansion of a wealth of virtues is like beholding the consort of a king.
The aforementioned perfection of qualities [is lost] for one whose splendor is struck down by misfortune.
Because she has become an object of hatred, she is considered equal to a female servant of a sage (ṛṣidāsī).
[8] She who possesses the excellence of qualities previously described, yet whose face is obscured by misfortune,
is held to be like a servant of a sage because she has become a locus of enmity.
One who relies on a base family is an object of pity, even if her splendor of virtues is as stainless as the moon—
just like a virtuous Brahmin woman who has fallen into the hands of a Caṇḍāla. (9) Possessing the splendor of qualities and free from stain, she is a cause for sorrow by relying on one of low birth.
A virtuous Brahmin wife is like a jewel held in the hand of one of low birth;
though they possess former qualities such as long life, health, beauty, and the rest, they are not honored when situated in poverty, just like fires situated in a cremation ground. [10]

These aforementioned qualities, such as long life, freedom from disease, and so forth, do not bring honor to the fool; he is like a person dwelling in a charnel ground. As it is said: "The perfection of qualities described leads only to the destruction of the fool."

Just as the abundance of fruit in plantains, lotus stalks, and bamboos serves only to bring about their own destruction, so too does the excellence of qualities already described lead to the ruin of the fool himself; it is like the ripening of the fruit of the plantain, the reed, and the bamboo.
Thus, the perfection of qualities as described, if lacking even a single limb,
will become fruitless— just like a science from which even a single syllable has been lost.
(12) Thus, the perfection of qualities as described, being impaired by the deficiency of even a single limb...
A science that lacks even a single syllable is equivalent to being fruitless;

however, knowledge that possesses the splendor of complete qualities and is devoid of missing letters will, through the perfection of yoga, bring about the attainment of the fruit in its entirety. [13]
The beauty of qualities fully perfected is like a science in which the syllables are complete;
from the accomplishment of application, the fruit is obtained, and that which is not incomplete will arise. Therefore, exert effort toward those qualities that are beautiful and complete.

Understand those causes by which these are attained as they are taught in the Sūtra: "Therefore, strive for these complete and beautiful qualities; learn from me what their causes are as explained in the Sūtra."
By releasing those condemned to death, by favoring others with the gift of life, and by abstaining from harming living beings,
one attains a long lifespan.

By abstaining from taking the lives of living beings, one will obtain a long life; by attending to the sick and providing physicians and medicines, and by refraining from harming living beings with clods of earth, sticks, and the like, one attains freedom from disease. [16]

By serving the sick, by providing excellent medicine, by summoning living beings with wealth and the like, and by practicing non-violence, one becomes free from disease. One attains beauty through the giving of ornaments and by cultivating freedom from anger.

The fruit of being free from envy is also proclaimed here as good fortune: "By relying on one who is without anger, one obtains a beautiful form; by giving ornaments, the fruit of being free from envy is fully explained as good fortune. [17]
By honoring and serving the virtuous, and by abandoning pride, one attains birth in a noble family;
and through generosity and the abstention from theft, one attains the abundance of enjoyments. (18) By honoring and serving the virtuous, and by abandoning pride, one becomes high-born.
By abstaining from stealing what has been given, one will obtain an abundance of wealth;
and through the diligent effort of asking correct questions such as "What is evil? What is virtuous?
and by the gift of the treatises on Dharma, one attains vast intelligence. [19]
By inquiring correctly about what is virtuous and what is non-virtuous,
and by bestowing Dharma treatises, one will attain vast intelligence. The Discourse on the Description of the Seven Qualities is complete.

The discourse on the complete exposition of the seven qualities, composed by the master Vasubandhu, is finished. It was translated, edited, and finalized by the Indian preceptor Paṇḍita Gaṅgādhara and the chief editor-translator, the monk Rinchen Zangpo.
